conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—short for Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the postpartum year, and it includes one question specifically about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us someone is in danger. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one is simple and there are no right or wrong answers. When you’re ready, we can start.

To begin: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say as much as you always could, not quite as much, definitely not so much now, or not at all?
I’ve still been able to laugh a little—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but I do find moments. So I’d say “not quite as much.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve still been able to laugh a little—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but I do find moments. So I’d say “not quite as much.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to help or when I get a quiet moment with the baby—but the excitement isn’t quite the same. I’d say “rather less than I used to.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Sometimes, yeah… like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m doing something wrong. It’s not every time, just occasionally.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I do notice myself getting anxious out of the blue—like I’ll suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing even when he’s right there sleeping fine. It’s not constant, but it happens.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, but there are moments—usually at night—when my heart starts racing and I imagine something bad happening to the baby. It passes pretty quickly, though.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… some days everything feels like a pile-up—feedings, diapers, laundry, trying to grab a shower—and I think, “How am I going to get through the next hour?” I haven’t felt totally out of control, but it’s definitely overwhelming at times.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve had trouble sleeping, but it’s more that I can’t shut my mind off—running through the baby’s schedule or worrying I’ll miss his cries—than feeling really unhappy. It’s not every night, maybe three or four times this week.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I’ve had patches of feeling down—like yesterday afternoon I just started crying while rocking the baby, but it lifted after an hour or so. It isn’t all day, but it pops up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I did cry once this week—just felt suddenly overwhelmed and teary for maybe half an hour—but it’s not a daily thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Screening Summary – Postpartum Period (self-report EPDS-style)

Symptoms / concerns endorsed
- Reduced enjoyment/pleasure (Q2, Q8)
- Episodic tearfulness, “patches of feeling down” (Q8, Q9)
- Sleep disturbance related to racing thoughts about baby (Q7)
- Anxiety/worry without clear trigger; brief nocturnal surges of fear (Q4, Q5)
- Periodic self-blame when baby is fussy (Q3)
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks (Q6)

Not endorsed
- Thoughts of self-harm (Q10)

Pattern
Mild-to-moderate mood and anxiety symptoms present several days per week; no safety concerns identified today. Findings suggestive of possible postpartum depression/anxiety requiring further evaluation.

Risk factors noted
- Fluctuating low mood and crying spells
- Sleep loss tied to ruminative worry
- Situational guilt and perceived coping deficits

Screening observation
Patient demonstrates sub-threshold but clinically significant mood and anxiety symptoms in the postpartum period; denies suicidal ideation. Continue monitoring and recommend formal assessment for postpartum depression/anxiety with standardized tool and/or clinician interview.
